title: Which Way Is Downhill?
key_insight: A derivative is a tiny test step on a foggy hill; a gradient collects those downhill clues when there are many directions.
body:
## Which Way Is Downhill?

You're on a foggy hill. You can't see far, but you can test a step downhill or uphill. That tiny test is a derivative—it tells you which way to go.

A model does the same thing with a weight instead of your foot: nudge it a little, then see whether the error goes up or down.

Move opposite the direction that increases error, and you're headed downhill. That is the basic idea behind training.
common_mistakes: Thinking a derivative is the average change over the whole curve — it describes the change right near one chosen point.
Assuming a positive derivative is always good — for an error score, training usually wants to move in the direction that lowers the score.
Treating a gradient as one number — it contains one local slope for each adjustable input.
mini_exercise: Estimate the slope of `y = x²` at `x = 2` using a step of `0.1`, then `0.01`. Compare both answers with the exact slope, which is `2 × x`.
real_world_usage: Every call to `loss.backward()` in PyTorch asks the framework to find how the loss changes with each trainable weight. Optimizers use those derivatives to update the model.
explain_back_prompt: Use the foggy-hill story to explain a derivative, a gradient, and why training moves opposite the gradient of error.
